title: Social Media Ad Sizes, Explained Simply | AIVideosUGC
description: Social media ad sizes for TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube, built with voice, captions, music, and a product link so each frame is ready to post.
h1: Social Media Ad Sizes: Which Shape Goes Where
lead: Social media ad sizes come down to the frame: 9:16 for a full phone screen, 1:1 for feeds, and 16:9 for wide screens. Start from a product link or a photo, and the file comes back already framed, with a script, captions, a voice, and a track when you want them.
secondary_keywords: square ads for the Facebook feed
summary: Make 9:16 first for full-screen phone ads, add 1:1 for feeds, and make 16:9 only when the screen is wide.

sections.h2: Social video formats shoppers already stop for
paras: Pick the format that shows one reason to buy. The shape comes after that.
Trend challenges. When a sound is moving, put the product inside that pattern and let the cut land on the beat. A hand snapping a stand open is enough.
How-to tips. Teach one use, such as a lid that does not leak when tipped. A short script becomes the picture, with a generated presenter or just the product.
A day with the product. A morning routine, a commute, a desk. Keep the product in the action from the first moment.
Reply clips. Answer a comment by showing the product doing the thing they asked about. It feels like a reply, and the offer stays readable.
A short list. Three reasons, said fast, with the product on screen the whole time. Good when people save posts to compare later.
Behind the packing table. Show the fill, the seal, or the unboxing. Shoppers trust a process they can see.
A calm lifestyle frame. The product in good light, on a real surface, for the grid. Mood carries it. The label still has to be true.
A short funny beat. One joke, then the product, readable. If the gag hides the item, it is the wrong joke.

sections.h2: A native frame for every social feed
paras: Each placement gets its own file, built at that shape. You do not crop a wide clip down by hand and hope the product survives.

YouTube and Shorts. Use 16:9 when the screen is wide, and 9:16 for Shorts. A tall file is its own job. Cutting the landscape version afterward often loses the product. See [YouTube Shorts](page:plat-youtube-shorts) for where the tall frame runs.
Instagram and Facebook. Reels wants 9:16. Do not drop the square feed file into that spot, or you get empty bands. The feed itself wants 1:1, and a carousel should keep every card the same shape.
TikTok. In-feed ads use 9:16. A 16:9 clip on an upright phone shrinks to a thin band, and the product looks small. Make the tall file with [AI UGC video ads](page:video-ads).
A professional feed. The same product can sit in a square or a wide post where people read more carefully. Keep the words large, and keep the claim identical to the product page.

sections.h2: Native specs that keep the product visible
paras: Match the shape to the screen, then check the crop before you spend. These are shapes, not a promise about pixel counts. Confirm the crop in the ad manager. Lengths are 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds, at 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits.
16:9, the wide frame. Use it for a laptop or a TV-style placement, a longer demo, or a desktop feed. It is a poor fit for a full phone screen.

9:16, the tall frame. This fills TikTok, Reels, Stories, and Shorts. The caption runs along the bottom, and the like and share buttons sit on the right. Keep the product and any words in the middle. Cover the bottom and the right side of your phone with your fingers. If you can still see the product and read the offer, the frame is safe.
1:1, the square frame. Use it for the Facebook and Instagram feeds, for a carousel, and whenever you are not sure which placement will run. A still of the same product can sit beside the video.

4:3 and 3:4, only when that placement lists them. If the ad manager does not list that shape, stay with 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9. All five shapes are available. For current Shorts file rules, see [YouTube Shorts ad specs](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/16041697?hl=en-GB).

sections.h2: Reasons to let the tool make each cut
paras: You skip the evening of trimming. The same photo can feed every placement, and each shape shows its credit cost before it starts.
See what is moving in your category. Put the product into a sound or a challenge while people still know it. You are not guessing from last month's post.
Borrow a pace you like. Paste a clip whose rhythm fits the product. The tool reads the hook and the pace, then builds your item into that rhythm. It does not copy someone else's footage.
Post without being on camera. Use a presenter from the [actor library](page:ai-actors), or show only the product. Anyone on screen is generated. Do not name them as a buyer.
Turn a page into a clip. Paste your product link, or a short page you wrote, and [URL to video](page:url-to-video) pulls the title, the photos, and the reason to buy into a tall clip with a voice.

sections.h2: How shops put this to work
paras: These are examples of how a shop would use it, not quotes from a customer.
Example. A home shop used to spend an evening cutting one clip. Now they paste the product page, take a 9:16 file and a 1:1 file as two jobs, and read both on a phone before they spend.

Example. A skincare shop needs a second opening for the same bottle. They keep the photo and the offer, change the first line, and run the two files together with the same audience and the same budget.

sections.h2: A setup for the product you actually sell
paras: The pace should match the product. A gag that hides the label is the wrong format.
Beauty and skincare. A routine, a texture, a before-and-after of the surface. Keep the shade honest when you hold the real item next to the screen.
Fashion. An outfit change on the beat, or the garment flat on a door and then worn. Do not invent a side the photo never showed.
Home and living. The product in the room it belongs in, plus one close frame of the joint, the cord, or the finish.
Food and drinks. The pour, the steam, the first bite. Six or ten seconds is often enough.
Jewelry. On a hand or a collar, with the clasp visible. A generated wearer is not a customer review.
Electronics and gadgets. One action, such as a stand unfolding or a case closing. Words stay in the middle so the buttons do not cover them.

sections.h2: Features that build the social cut
paras: The maker covers the chores that used to live in three different apps.
A trend watch for your category. It points at a sound and a hook that fit the product, so you are not posting last month's joke.
Presenters, or none. Pick someone from the actor library, make one for the brand, or leave people out. Generated people stay unnamed.
Cuts that follow the beat. Choose a track from the ad music library and the edits land on that rhythm. Confirm the placement allows the track before you spend.
A script you can edit. It is written from the product page, aimed at a reply, and you can change the line before the job runs.
A link in, a clip out. A product URL or a short page becomes a narrated vertical video. [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) is the path when you already have the still.

Finish in one place. Captions, the voice, and the track are in the editor. Restyle the captions, run a batch of openings from the same photo, and publish to TikTok or Meta in one step, or download the file. Downloads have no watermark. A developer can start the same job through the API from your shop system. Each file is its own job, and a failed job returns the credits.

sections.h2: From a link to today's post in 5 moves
paras: You are not cutting frame by frame. Five moves, then a phone check.
Paste a product URL, a clip whose pace you want, or a photo of the item.
Read the pace. The tool notes the hook, the speed, and where the product must stay visible.
Build the shape you picked. The cut follows the track. Frames are 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4.
A second shape is another job. It is not included in the first one.
Hold attention with captions, a voice, and another beat. Keep words off the bottom and the right.
Download a file with no watermark, or publish to TikTok or Meta. Then read it on your phone.
The cost shows first: 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds.

faq.q: Can I turn a longer clip into a TikTok, Reel, or Short?
faq.a: Yes. Ask for 9:16 and a length of 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. The useful moment is framed for the phone, with room for captions. Do not slice a wide file down yourself. That often cuts the product off.

faq.q: Can I post without showing my face?
faq.a: Yes. Use a presenter from the actor library, or show only the product. Anyone on screen is generated. Do not present them as a customer or a reviewer.

faq.q: Are the music and the voiceover safe to use in an ad?
faq.a: The music library is built for ads, and the voice is generated. Still confirm that the placement allows that track before you spend. A song that is fine on a personal post is often not cleared for advertising.

faq.q: Can the edit follow the beat?
faq.a: Yes. Pick a track and the cuts follow that rhythm. Lengths stay 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds, at 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits.

faq.q: Can I start from a product page?
faq.a: Yes. Paste the product URL. The title, the photos, and the reason to buy come in with it, and you can edit the script before the job runs. A second shape is a separate job. A 10-second clip is 40 credits.

faq.q: Can I change how the captions look?
faq.a: Yes. Restyle them in the editor, and keep the words in the middle. The account name, the caption, and the buttons sit along the bottom and the right edge.

faq.q: Can the same ad run in another language?
faq.a: Yes. The same script can be captioned and spoken in another language, without a second shoot. Use 4:3 or 3:4 only when the ad manager lists that shape. Downloads have no watermark.
